rationale: A wins because it has editorial discipline: three real shapes, no padded pricing hobbyhorse, and proof gates that would keep a founder from embarrassing themselves. Its strongest headline, "Replit Built a Platform to Teach Coding. Now It's Selling a Tool That Skips It.", gives a reporter a real tension. B has good bones, especially reliability, but "You pay per build" invents a billing unit from thin air, and that is how a decent angle set gets sent back to the shop.
gaps_in_A: "Replit contradicting its own founding premise" overstates the update. We know Replit is used heavily in education, not that teaching coding was its founding premise.
"Replit explicitly declines to disclose reliability rates" turns non-disclosure into an active refusal. The facts say reliability is not disclosed, not that Replit was asked and declined.

"the market has moved from AI that assists developers to AI that replaces the development workflow" is too grand for one launch. A correctly asks for comparable offerings, but the headline argument should not outrun that proof.
gaps_in_B: "from one English sentence" is invented. The update says plain-English description, not a single sentence.
"You pay per build" is the worst miss in the set. Usage-based pricing is disclosed; the unit of usage is not.
"people who can't code - which is most students before a course" smuggles in an education assumption the update does not support.
"Without real numbers this is a topic, not a story" is exactly right, which means the pricing angle should have been refused or quarantined, not promoted as a kept angle.
